authors: McIntyre, A.; Sinclair, J.; Page-Smith, J.; Ziekemijjer, P.; Ellis, N.
title: Overview and Outcomes of Victoria’s Passing Distance Cycling Safety Public Education Campaign
design: Public education campaign with repeated cross-sectional surveys and a naturalistic PassBox before/after passing-distance sample in Melbourne.
sample: repeat riders: 18; all pass events approx: 20000; matched rider location events approx: 13000; survey waves n: [614, 745, 336]; unit: cyclists, passing events, and survey respondents
endpoint: Instrumented passing distance and close-pass rates; survey-reported awareness, understanding, and support for passing-distance rules.
finding: Regression modeling on matched cyclists and locations reported a significantly lower 1.99% rate of close passing after the campaign. The report does not specify whether 1.99% is relative or percentage-point change. Survey changes in support/understanding were small and several returned toward baseline by March.
limits: Extended abstract omits close-pass definition, regression specification, standard error, and confidence interval; no untreated comparison; unmatched seasonal windows; only 18 repeat cyclists; no crash endpoint. Do not convert 1.99% or attribute it to a specific ad.
access: Full extended abstract in proceedings; no detailed technical report located

authors: Mills, A.; Loskorn, J.; Brady, J.; Duthie, J.; Machemehl, R.
title: Effects of Bicycles May Use Full Lane Signs on Bicyclist and Motorist Behavior along Multi-Lane Facilities
design: Traffic-camera before/after observations at two Austin multi-lane road sites after BMUFL sign installation.
sample: passing events: At Lamar Boulevard the table lists 61 before and 45 after passing events; the same row's total is arithmetically inconsistent. Pleasant Valley had too few post-installation passing events for a useful analysis.; unit: vehicle-bicycle events at two sites
endpoint: Observed vehicle–bicycle passing distance, lane changes and encroachment; cyclist lane and sidewalk use.
finding: At Lamar, measured space among passes without a lane change increased; the share within 3 ft fell from 44% to 0%. Adjacent-lane encroachment increased from 77% to 97% (p=.030). At Pleasant Valley, cyclist use of the full lane decreased and sidewalk/avoidance behavior increased, but passing data were too sparse for a stable estimate.
limits: Small, uncontrolled before/after study; a passing ordinance was adopted during the study period; report did not record whether adjacent lanes were occupied; event table includes an internal arithmetic inconsistency; no crash endpoint.
access: Full city-sponsored report

authors: Gauld, C.; Craft, T.; Stepnik, M.
title: Investigating the efficacy of social norms messages to reduce smartphone use among young drivers
design: Online survey experiment randomly assigning young drivers to descriptive-, subjective-, or injunctive-norm messages.
sample: 136 young New South Wales drivers; 92 women and 44 men.
endpoint: Immediate message comprehension, stated intention, perceived message effectiveness, message rejection, and third-person effect.
finding: No message-type effect on intention (F(2,130)=1.02, p=.365). Message effectiveness had an omnibus difference (F(2,130)=4.64, p=.011), but no pairwise differences survived Bonferroni adjustment. Twelve of 52 respondents (23%) interpreted the descriptive-norm message in the opposite direction.
limits: Smartphone use rather than cyclist passing; immediate self-report, no no-message control and no observed driving behavior. The sample was predominantly female; comprehension result should not be generalized as proof of cycling-message failure.
access: Open full journal article PDF.

authors: Mulvaney, C. A.; Kendrick, D.; Watson, M. C.; Coupland, C. A. C.
title: Increasing child pedestrian and cyclist visibility: cluster randomised controlled trial
design: Cluster-randomized trial; free reflective/fluorescent slap wrap and reflective sticker plus educational material versus control; observers recorded use at baseline, one week and eight weeks.
sample: 377 children aged 7–9 from 20 Nottingham school classes; pedestrian and cyclist visibility behaviors combined.
endpoint: Observed use of fluorescent or reflective visibility aids by child pedestrians and cyclists.
finding: Observed use of any visibility aid was higher in the intervention arm at one week (adjusted OR 59.5, 95% CI 18.5–191.0) and eight weeks (adjusted OR 5.9, 95% CI 3.4–10.4).
limits: Equipment and education bundled; wide one-week CI; short winter follow-up; mixed pedestrian/cyclist sample; no collision or injury outcome and no isolated leaflet effect.
access: Full article PDF available

authors: Hodgson, C.; Worth, J.
title: Research into the impact of Bikeability training on children's ability to perceive and appropriately respond to hazards when cycling on the road
design: Non-randomized comparison of trained and comparison pupils, repeated on-screen hazard-perception/response quiz and a separate practical assessment of trained pupils only.
sample: 29 schools in the overall evaluation. Quiz phase 2: 66 trained and 76 comparison pupils; phase 3: 101 trained and 53 comparison pupils. Practical assessment: 75 trained pupils at phase 2 and 64 at phase 3, from six schools.
endpoint: Screen-based hazard-perception and response quiz scores; practical cycling-assessment scores and reported cycling frequency.
finding: Reported quiz effect sizes were 1.58 at phase 2 and 1.60 at phase 3; no confidence intervals were reported for these estimates. The quiz difference persisted more than two months. In the trained-only practical cohort, the mean score fell by 1.6 points from phase 2 to phase 3. Pupils reported no increase in cycling frequency.
limits: School access/training not randomized. Quiz is knowledge/performance in a screen-based task; no injury endpoint. Practical assessment had no comparison group and smaller follow-up sample; the decline is not a controlled estimate of retention.
access: Full NFER report and appendices available

authors: Concepts of Change; Ipsos Social Research
title: Reducing Car Dooring: The role of stickers as visual reminders
design: Qualitative street recruitment, four focus groups comparing sticker and conversation prompts, and four in-depth interviews.
sample: approached: 218; eligible: 124; agreed recontact: 60; focus groups: 4; in depth interviews: 4; sticker recipients at follow up: 11; unit: Melbourne street-interview participants
endpoint: Participants’ reported perceptions of dooring and stickers, recall and use of the sticker, and responses to prompts.
finding: Of 11 sticker recipients interviewed at follow-up, four initially did not recall receiving a sticker and one reported using it. Participants said stickers could fade into the background and were unlikely to work alone; face-to-face questions appeared to alert people to the issue.
limits: Qualitative and self-selected sample; four groups and small follow-up; no randomized causal estimate, observed door-opening behavior, or dooring/crash outcome.
access: Full report by Concepts of Change with Ipsos Social Research, prepared for Road Safety Action Group Inner Melbourne; evaluates VicRoads stickers

authors: Crundall, D.; van Loon, E.
title: Improving attitudes towards vulnerable road users
design: Randomized online video intervention with cyclist- and horse-focused personal stories and an unrelated road-safety video control; pre/post attitude and stated passing-distance/speed questions.
sample: total: 344; population: UK drivers age 18-78; unit: survey participants
endpoint: Explicit and implicit attitudes toward cyclists and horse riders; stated passing distance and speed.
finding: Explicit attitudes improved toward the road-user represented in the video; intended passing distance increased and intended passing speed decreased. No implicit-attitude effect was found. Changes were specific to the target shown; cyclist videos did not improve attitudes toward horse riders and horse videos did not improve attitudes toward cyclists.
limits: Immediate self-reported and image-slider outcomes only; no actual driving or crash outcomes; online sample with positive baseline attitudes; potential ceiling effects and reactance/blame in some comments.
access: Full evaluation report plus journal abstract

authors: Crundall, D.; van Loon, E.
title: Revisiting attitude change sixteen months after vulnerable road user empathy videos: Look Out For Laura follow-up evaluation
design: Approximately 16-month follow-up of original randomized cyclist/horse empathy-video groups using repeated online attitude and stated passing-distance/speed items.
sample: completed follow up text: 224; condition table total: 223; unit: follow-up survey participants
endpoint: Follow-up explicit attitudes toward cyclists and horse riders; stated passing distance and speed.
finding: Immediate targeted attitude and intended-distance effects were replicated in the retained subset, but no intervention advantage over baseline remained nearly 16 months later. In the reduced subset, cyclist-video effects on stated passing speed did not show the same immediate group-specific pattern. No negative rebound was found.
limits: Condition table totals 223 although report text says 224 completed; only 65% of original sample completed follow-up; online intended behavior, not actual driving; the interval does not reveal when the immediate gains faded.
access: Full evaluation report

authors: Large, D. R.; Choo, M. C.; Houghton, R.
title: Validating Dutch Reach: A Preliminary Evaluation of Far-Hand Door Opening and its Impact on Car Drivers’ Head Movements
design: Repeated-measures psychophysics experiment in one right-hand-drive Honda Civic; head motion measured during near-hand and far-hand door opening in driver and passenger seats.
sample: participants: 10; door openings: 80; unit: participants and repeated door-opening trials
endpoint: Measured head rotation during near-hand and far-hand door opening in driver and passenger seats.
finding: Driver-seat mean head rotation was 5.81 degrees for near-hand versus 9.20 degrees for far-hand opening. No comparable hand effect was found in the passenger seat.
limits: Preliminary single-vehicle experiment; omitted a rear-hazard detection task; no behavior in traffic, cyclist detection, dooring incident, or injury endpoint; far-hand opening was only one component of the broader technique.
access: Full author-posted conference paper and institutional record

authors: Delbosc, A.; Naznin, F.; Haslam, N.; Haworth, N.
title: Dehumanization of cyclists predicts self-reported aggressive behaviour toward them: A pilot study
design: Cross-sectional convenience survey
sample: Australian respondents
endpoint: Humanity ratings and self-reported aggression
finding: Lower humanity ratings associated with reported aggression.
limits: Association only; no campaign intervention or measured road behavior.
access: Full author manuscript PDF in local collection; abstract and association results checked

authors: Kendrick, D.; Royal, S.
title: Cycle helmet ownership and use; a cluster randomised controlled trial in primary school children in deprived areas
design: Cluster randomized trial comparing an educational pack plus free-helmet order form with the same pack/order form plus assembly, lesson, and cycling-event invitation.
sample: 28 primary schools in deprived areas; 1,213 Year 5 children aged 9–10.
endpoint: Cycle helmet ownership and wearing.
finding: The pack arm was not statistically distinguishable from the multifaceted arm for ownership (reported OR 1.51, 95% CI 0.50–4.58) or wearing (OR 0.98, 0.57–1.68). Ownership increased from baseline in both arms; the pack arm also had a significant baseline-to-follow-up increase in wearing. Authors report reduced inequality in helmet ownership.
limits: Both arms included access to a free helmet; not leaflet-only versus no intervention. Wide CIs do not demonstrate equivalence. Outcomes were ownership and wearing, not crashes or injuries.
access: Open full-text trial

authors: Department for Transport / THINK!
title: THINK! Cycling Evaluation 2016: Don’t get caught campaign
design: Pre/post cyclist surveys; no randomized control
sample: 573 pre; 500 post
endpoint: Recall, self-report, blame and participation intentions
finding: Some respondents perceived rider blame or anticipated cycling less.
limits: Survey reactions are not observed riding or causal injury effects.
access: Original official evaluation PDF

authors: DiMaggio, C.; Brady, J.; Li, G.
title: Association of the Safe Routes to School program with school-age pedestrian and bicyclist injury risk in Texas
design: Observational program evaluation with adult trend comparison
sample: Texas statewide injury series
endpoint: Combined pedestrian/bicyclist injuries
finding: Decline associated with program period; causal attribution unresolved.
limits: Pre-existing decline and secular trends; combined mode endpoint; not education-only.
access: Open full article

authors: Box, E.
title: Highway Code Intervention Evaluation Report
design: Randomized three-arm online pre/post/follow-up evaluation of the Co-Pilot Highway Code film against two road-safety film controls. The film covered updated rules for different road users; measured cycling-specific knowledge included overtaking distance, while the measured turning-priority question concerned a pedestrian waiting to cross as a driver turns into a side road.
sample: pre post: 254; follow up: 210; population: licensed UK drivers age 25+; unit: survey participants
endpoint: Highway Code knowledge, including pedestrian turning priority and cyclist passing distance; self-reported intentions, perceived control and norms.
finding: Correct responses to the pedestrian-priority rule for a driver turning into a side road rose in the intervention group from 67% at baseline to 99% immediately and 87% at 4-6 weeks. Correct responses to the cyclist overtaking-distance item rose from 37% to 73% and were 51% at follow-up. Group-by-time analyses favored the intervention over controls. Self-reported intentions, perceived behavioral control, and social norms also showed group-by-time signals.
limits: Questionnaire knowledge and self-reported behavioral determinants, not observed driving or passing; the turning knowledge item was about pedestrian priority, not cyclist priority; online Prolific sample; short follow-up; the evaluation was self-funded by Co-Pilot, the intervention developer; no crash endpoint.
access: Full report

authors: Hess, G.; Peterson, M. N.
title: Bicycles May Use Full Lane Signage Communicates U.S. Roadway Rules and Increases Perception of Safety
design: Web-based randomized scenario survey assigning respondents to BMUFL, Share the Road, shared-lane markings, or unsigned-roadway conditions; outcomes were rule comprehension and perceived safety.
sample: responses received: 1978; analyzed: 1824; unit: U.S. survey respondents
endpoint: Correct recognition of bicycle lane-use and passing rules and perceived safety in hypothetical road scenarios.
finding: BMUFL improved correct recognition of lane-use and passing rules in most scenarios and increased perceived safety. Share the Road responses did not differ significantly from unsigned-roadway responses. No road behavior or crash outcome was measured.
limits: Twitter-recruited convenience sample; hypothetical image scenarios; responses measure understanding and perception rather than actual behavior; some reported comparisons use p<.10.
access: Full peer-reviewed open-access article

authors: Lahrmann, H.; Madsen, T. K. O.; Olesen, A. V.; Madsen, J. C. O.; Hels, T.
title: The effect of a yellow bicycle jacket on cyclist accidents
design: One-year randomized trial of yellow high-visibility jacket versus regular clothing, using monthly self-reported accidents; corrected rates account for apparent differential under-reporting.
sample: 6,793 volunteer Danish adult cyclists: 3,402 test and 3,391 control; regular cyclists riding at least three times per week in summer.
endpoint: Monthly self-reported bicycle accidents, including multiparty personal-injury accidents; reported jacket use.
finding: For multiparty personal-injury accidents more severe than bruising, uncorrected accident-rate ratio (ARR) 0.53 (95% CI 0.37–0.77). After correction for apparent reporting bias, ARR 0.62 (0.39–1.00), marked significant by the paper. Average reported jacket use was about 77%.
limits: Unblinded, volunteer and frequent adult Danish cyclists; monthly self-report. Correction assumes single-party injury reports indicate reporting bias for multiparty events; estimate is equipment efficacy, not campaign/message effect.
access: Open full-text author/institutional PDF and publisher article page

authors: Pless, I. B.; Verreault, R.; Tenina, S.
title: A case-control study of pedestrian and bicyclist injuries in childhood
design: Montreal hospital case-control study; blinded parent interviews and tests; logistic regression adjusted for age, gender, and socioeconomic area.
sample: 200 traffic-injured children aged 0–14 (MAIS score at least 2) and 400 uninjured hospital controls; pedestrians and bicyclists combined.
endpoint: Traffic injury among child pedestrians and bicyclists in relation to parental supervision and other risk factors.
finding: Poor parental supervision was associated with injury; the study reports OR 2.6 (95% CI 1.5–4.7) for poor versus good supervision. It also identifies parental education, family accident history, and unsafe environment as relevant associations.
limits: Mixed pedestrian/cyclist outcome, observational design, hospital controls, and no tested supervision message or intervention. Does not establish an age threshold for independent cycling or prove supervision alone prevents injury.
access: Open full-text article; exact estimate also indexed in article text

authors: Nawaz, I.; Cuenen, A.; Ahmed, T.; Zeb, A.; Wets, G.; Janssens, D.
title: Road Safety education for children and adolescents: A systematic review of effectiveness, methods, and challenges
design: PRISMA-described systematic review searching Scopus, PubMed, and Web of Science; studies published 2004–2024 across multiple road-user types and education formats.
sample: 46 studies across 26 countries; the publisher abstract does not give a participant total or cyclist-only subgroup size.
endpoint: Reported changes in road-safety knowledge, attitudes and behavior in included education studies.
finding: The authors report that 83% of studies found significant knowledge improvement, 71% positive attitude changes, and 68% measurable behavior improvement. The outcomes included pedestrian and cycling behaviors; the abstract does not provide pooled effect sizes or a bicycle-specific crash/injury estimate.
limits: Percentages count studies with reported positive findings; they are not pooled effect sizes or proportions of children helped. Broad road-safety scope, heterogeneous methods, and no cyclist-specific injury conclusion in the accessible abstract. Full text not accessed.
access: Publisher article page and abstract; full text paywalled/not accessed

authors: Ipsos UK
title: An evaluation of the ADI Cycle Awareness Pilot
design: Randomized delayed-access trial of online cycle-awareness training for approved driving instructors; learner-driver access was also offered but not completed.
sample: recruited baseline: 2339; treatment baseline: 1169; control baseline: 1170; endline comparison: 629; endline treatment: 179; endline control: 450; learner drivers registered: 33; learner drivers completed: 0; unit: instructors and learner drivers
endpoint: Instructor attitudes toward cyclists, awareness and perceptions, and self-reported driving and teaching intentions.
finding: Only 2 of 13 cyclist-attitude items showed a statistically significant treatment effect: cyclist-as-nuisance was lower by 0.33 scale points; cyclist-fault-for-crashes was lower by 0.23, marginal after Bonferroni adjustment. Awareness of Bikeability increased. No driving behavior was measured.
limits: Only 15% of recruited ADIs completed the learning and endline; severe attrition and unbalanced endline samples; no learner-driver completions; attitudes and intended teaching rather than observed driving; no crash endpoint.
access: Full Ipsos UK report dated December 2022 and appendices; published by Department for Transport on GOV.UK on 31 October 2024

authors: Kwan, I.; Mapstone, J.
title: Interventions for increasing pedestrian and cyclist visibility for the prevention of death and injuries
design: Cochrane systematic review of randomized visibility-aid trials; searches last updated May 2009.
sample: 35 papers reporting 42 detection/recognition trials, 1,171 participants; no eligible crash/injury trials were found in the review search.
endpoint: Driver detection and recognition tasks, plus cyclist/pedestrian collision and injury endpoints where available.
finding: Some fluorescent materials improved daytime detection; lamps, flashing lights, and retroreflective materials improved detection or recognition at night. No trial measured crash or injury reduction at the time of the review.
limits: Most outcomes were surrogate visibility tasks; only a subset directly involved cyclists; diverse interventions and settings prevented a pooled effect estimate. Search predates newer equipment trials.
access: Open full review and Cochrane summary.

authors: Madsen, J. C. O.; Andersen, T.; Lahrmann, H. S.
title: Safety effects of permanent running lights for bicycles: A controlled experiment
design: Controlled 12-month trial of bicycle-mounted permanent running lights; accident rates compared between a treatment and control group.
sample: 3,845 cyclists in Odense, Denmark: 1,845 light-equipped treatment bicycles and 2,000 controls.
endpoint: Self-reported bicycle accidents and personal injuries, including multiparty accidents, per person-month.
finding: The authors report 19% lower incidence of all recorded self-reported bicycle accidents with personal injury in the light group, measured per person-month; abstract also reports a significant reduction in multiparty accidents.
limits: Equipment trial, not a messaging intervention. Accident data self-reported online; report itself discusses potential reporting shortcomings. Person-month denominator is not distance cycled; no CI in accessible abstract; one Danish setting.
access: Original full journal article PDF supplied by reader; indexed PubMed record.

authors: Kay, J. J.; Savolainen, P. T.; Gates, T. J.; Datta, T. K.
title: Driver behavior during bicycle passing maneuvers in response to a Share the Road sign treatment
design: Before/after field study of passing behavior at two similar rural two-lane highway segments; observed vehicle lateral position and speed with and without the Share the Road sign treatment and in settings with/without centerline rumble strips.
sample: Observed passing events on two rural two-lane road segments; see original article for model-specific samples.
endpoint: Observed vehicle lateral position, passing speed, cyclist buffer distance and crowding probability.
finding: The sign shifted vehicles away from rightmost lane positions and reduced passing speed by 2.5 mph (4.0 km/h); it did not significantly affect mean buffer distance or crowding probability. Centerline rumble strips tended to shift vehicles closer to cyclists, marginally.
limits: Specific high-speed rural sites; field before/after design; no crash endpoint. Speed, lateral position, buffer distance and crowding are distinct outcomes.
access: Full original journal PDF supplied by reader; abstract and field results checked

authors: Sinclair, J.; Nolan, J.
title: Do minimum passing distance laws for cyclists change driver behaviour?
design: PassBox before/after instrumented passing-distance study in Perth following a minimum passing-distance law introduced alongside an advertising campaign.
sample: cyclists: 70; unit: cyclists; passing-event count not stated in the accessible abstract
endpoint: Instrumented motor-vehicle passing distance before and after the combined law and advertising change.
finding: For roads at or below 60 km/h, the closest 5% of passes were 10 cm farther from cyclists after the combined law/advertising change (95% CI 2-19 cm). No effect was observed on roads at or above 70 km/h.
limits: Combined law/advertising change, not campaign-only; pre/post observation; closest 5% estimate rather than average. Local preprint reports 12 cm (4.9–19.0); published abstract reports 10 cm (2–19). Use published value.
access: Local author preprint plus published journal abstract; published abstract used for the 10 cm estimate

authors: Olivier, J.; Creighton, P.
title: Bicycle injuries and helmet use: a systematic review and meta-analysis
design: Systematic review and multivariate meta-regression of studies reporting medically diagnosed injury and known helmet use among cyclists involved in a crash or fall.
sample: 43 eligible studies; 40 included in meta-analysis, with data from more than 64,000 injured cyclists.
endpoint: Head, serious head, face, fatal head and neck injuries among cyclists involved in a crash or fall, by helmet use.
finding: Helmet use associated with lower odds of head injury (OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.42–0.57), serious head injury (0.31, 0.25–0.37), face injury (0.67, 0.56–0.81), and fatal head injury (0.35, 0.14–0.88). Neck injury association was unclear (0.96, 0.74–1.25).
limits: Primarily observational injury studies and conditional on crash/fall involvement; estimates concern injury mitigation, not crash prevention or effect of a helmet campaign. Residual confounding remains possible.
access: PubMed abstract and open full-text copy available from author/institutional sources

authors: Carlin, J. B.; Taylor, P.; Nolan, T.
title: School based bicycle safety education and bicycle injuries in children: a case-control study
design: Population-based case-control evaluation of exposure to a school bicycle-safety course among injured and uninjured children.
sample: 148 injury cases and 130 controls aged 9–14 years.
endpoint: Child bicycle injury associated with exposure to a school bicycle-safety education course.
finding: No evidence of a protective effect: OR 1.64 (95% CI 0.98–2.75). Among boys, OR 2.0 (95% CI 1.1–3.8). Authors hypothesized inadvertent risk-taking or inadequate supervision as possible explanations.
limits: Observational association cannot show the course caused harm; potential confounding, selection, and differences in exposure. Historical program and setting limit current transfer. Authors' proposed mechanism was not tested.
access: Open full-text article PDF and PubMed record

authors: Lankarani, K. B.; Akbari, M.; Razzaghi, A.; Taghi Heydari, S.; Vali, M.; Tabrizi, R.; Sullman, M. J. M.
title: Mass media campaigns to increase the use of bicycle helmets: A systematic review and meta-analysis
design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of mass-media campaigns aimed at bicycle helmet use; searches covered January 2000 to February 2022.
sample: Eight eligible articles; participant totals and study-level designs are not reported in the accessible abstract.
endpoint: Bicycle helmet use following mass-media campaigns in included studies.
finding: Pooled helmet-use OR 3.77 (95% CI 1.16–12.20); I²=99.9% (heterogeneity p<0.001). Abstract reports pooled p<0.001, which is not readily consistent with the displayed CI under a conventional two-sided Wald calculation. The endpoint is helmet wearing, not injury.
limits: Extreme heterogeneity and only eight articles make the pooled magnitude unstable; campaigns and comparison designs vary and may include other components. Do not use as a campaign forecast. Full article text not accessed for this review.
access: Publisher/indexed abstract; full article paywalled/not accessed

authors: Reymond, L.; Rérat, P.
title: Blaming Cyclists, Invisibilising Drivers: How Motonormativity Shapes Swiss Media Collision Reports
design: Content analysis of newspaper articles and coded headline/body sentences about cyclist–motorist collisions.
sample: 204 articles from six French-language Swiss newspapers, published 2020–2024; 179 headlines and 311 body-text sentences coded.
endpoint: Presence of an explicit agent, narrative focus, vehicle/person references, episodic/systemic framing, and language patterns.
finding: Explicit agents appeared in 27% of headlines; cyclists were the focus of 83% of headlines; motorists appeared in 42% and were usually referred to as vehicles (82%); 93% of stories used an episodic frame.
limits: Describes one language, country, and newspaper sample. Content analysis does not measure audience interpretation, causality, driver behavior, or campaign effectiveness.
access: Open full article, tables, and data files at Findings.

authors: Tannenbaum, M. B.; Hepler, J.; Zimmerman, R. S.; Saul, L.; Jacobs, S.; Wilson, K.; Albarracín, D.
title: Appealing to fear: A meta-analysis of fear appeal effectiveness and theories
design: Cross-domain meta-analysis of experimental fear appeals with comparison groups and attitude, intention, or behavior outcomes.
sample: 127 papers, 248 independent samples, N=27,372.
endpoint: Composite and separate attitudes, intentions, and behaviors across diverse health and safety topics.
finding: Small positive mean composite effect, random-effects d=.29 (95% CI .22–.35). Efficacy statements and one-time rather than repeated behaviors moderated effectiveness.
limits: Not a cyclist or road-safety campaign estimate; pooled outcomes and behaviors span many domains. It does not establish that graphic imagery helps or that a fear appeal is safe for every audience.
access: Open full text at PubMed Central; publisher PDF also publicly available.

authors: Michie, S.; van Stralen, M. M.; West, R.
title: The behaviour change wheel: A new method for characterising and designing behaviour change interventions
design: Framework synthesis and development
sample: 19 frameworks identified
endpoint: Intervention design framework
finding: Capability, opportunity and motivation organize barrier diagnosis.
limits: Not a cyclist intervention trial or an efficacy guarantee.
access: Open full article

authors: Rhodes, N.; Shulman, H. C.; McClaran, N.
title: Changing norms: A meta-analytic integration of research on social norms appeals
design: Meta-analysis of experimental social-norm manipulations with comparison groups.
sample: 110 articles; sample totals vary across outcome sets.
endpoint: Attitudes, perceived norms, intentions, and behavior across multiple topics and settings.
finding: Small average effects with significant heterogeneity. Fixed-effect behavior estimates were d=.10 for descriptive appeals (k=59) and d=.34 for injunctive appeals (k=11).
limits: Broad cross-domain evidence, not cycling or traffic passing; effects depend on design, population, message, and outcome. Do not use the averages to forecast a cyclist message.
access: Author manuscript publicly available; publisher record available.

authors: Haworth, N.; Delbosc, A.; Schramm, A.; Haslam, N.
title: How might advertising campaigns rehumanize cyclists?
design: ACT minimum-passing-distance poster survey experiment comparing four designs: photo versus graphic and front versus rear view; photo/graphic comparison was within-person, with photo presented first to all respondents.
sample: 267 usable survey responses.
endpoint: Dehumanization/humanization scale ratings, attitudes toward cyclists, clarity, memorability, and perceived effectiveness.
finding: Photographs produced small changes on humanization/dehumanization ratings but no overall attitude improvement. There was no overall front/rear main effect, but drivers rated the front-view cyclist more positively than the rear-view cyclist; cyclists did not show this pattern. Graphic versions received higher clarity, memorability, and perceived-effectiveness ratings. No actual driving was measured.
limits: Convenience online sample from one jurisdiction; fixed photo-first order; self-report ratings and one local passing-rule message; no measured recall, driver behavior, or crashes. Findings do not test AI-generated imagery.
access: Local author preprint; published journal abstract and full ACT project report. Local preprint is not the final peer-reviewed article.

authors: Owen, R.; Kendrick, D.; Mulvaney, C.; Coleman, T.; Royal, S.
title: Non-legislative interventions for the promotion of cycle helmet wearing by children
design: Cochrane systematic review of randomized and controlled before-after studies
sample: 29 studies; 11 in observed-wearing pool
endpoint: Observed helmet wearing; self-reported wearing/ownership
finding: Observed wearing favored intervention; OR2.08 (95%CI1.29-3.34).
limits: Heterogeneous mixed designs; observed-wearing RCT-only pool (3 studies) uncertain, OR0.99, CI0.18-5.63. Components not randomized; wearing, not injury.
access: Open full review

authors: Prabhakharan, P.; Bennett, J. M.; Hurden, A.; Crundall, D.
title: The efficacy of hazard perception training and education: A systematic review and meta-analysis
design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of hazard-perception training across road-user groups
sample: Cyclist subgroup: seven study samples from five papers; two retention checks at three weeks
endpoint: Video-based hazard-perception skills; cyclist road behavior was not assessed
finding: Cyclist pooled Hedges g 0.97 (95% CI 0.52–1.42), k=7; considerable heterogeneity I-squared 87.01%. Two studies found performance above pre-training at three weeks.
limits: Varied skill tasks and training methods, substantial heterogeneity; cyclist findings concern video-based hazard performance, not everyday behavior or injuries; brief retention follow-up.
access: Original full journal PDF supplied by reader; cyclist results in sections 3.6.1–3.6.2 checked

authors: Blomberg, R. D.; Wright, T. J.; Van Houten, R.; Finstad, K.; Thomas, F. D.
title: Evaluating High-Visibility Enforcement of Bicycle Passing Laws
design: Two-city repeated before/after evaluation of high-visibility enforcement combined with city publicity; police used ultrasonic devices with staged riders and volunteer cyclists.
sample: daytime passes: 38886; knoxville passes: 19527; grand rapids passes: 19359; unit: instrumented vehicle-bicycle passing events
endpoint: Instrumented passing distances and proportions of passes below legal thresholds for staged and volunteer riders.
finding: Grand Rapids volunteer passes under 5 ft fell from 26.01% to 18.17% at the last wave (p<.001). Knoxville staged passes under 3 ft fell from 4.98% to 3.11% (p=.017). Several volunteer subgroup changes were not significant. No crash outcome was measured.
limits: Publicity and police enforcement were bundled; no untreated comparison city; before/after design; staged and volunteer riders differ; measurement activity itself may have reminded drivers of the campaign. Do not attribute effects to publicity or posters alone.
access: Full government report and metadata page

authors: Carey, R. N.; McDermott, D. T.; Sarma, K. M.
title: The impact of threat appeals on fear arousal and driver behavior: A meta-analysis of experimental research 1990–2011
design: Meta-analysis of experimental driver-message studies published 1990–2011.
sample: 13 studies; 71 effects; total N=3,044. Fear was measured in four studies, n=619.
endpoint: Self-reported fear arousal and pooled driving behavior/intention outcomes, including lab/simulator and self-report measures.
finding: Threat appeals increased fear (r=.64, p<.01). The pooled driving outcome was not statistically significant (r=.03, p=.17; approximately 95% CI −.01 to .07).
limits: High heterogeneity; not bicycle-message-specific; no actual cyclist passing or bicycle crash outcomes. Nonsignificance is not an equivalence finding. Graphic/shock imagery was not isolated.
access: Open full text at PLOS ONE and PubMed Central.

authors: Phillips, R. O.; Ulleberg, P.; Vaa, T.
title: Meta-analysis of the effect of road safety campaigns on accidents
design: Meta-analysis/meta-regression of campaign evaluations with crash outcomes.
sample: 67 studies, 119 crash-effect estimates, 12 countries, 1975–2007.
endpoint: Road crashes across varied road-safety topics and campaign packages.
finding: Adjusted weighted average was about a 9% crash reduction (95% interval about 6%–12% fewer crashes). Personal communication and roadside media were associated with stronger effects in between-study analyses.
limits: Not cyclist-only and not print-only; substantial heterogeneity. Delivery components were not randomized, and the authors caution against using one average to forecast a new campaign.
access: Original full journal article PDF supplied by reader; PubMed record.

authors: Saleem, T.; et al.
title: Crash-based evaluation of the Watch for Me NC program
design: Empirical-Bayes county before-after program evaluation
sample: 29 treatment; 71 reference counties
endpoint: Pedestrian and bicycle crashes analyzed separately
finding: Bicycle conclusion inconclusive under alternative exposure models.
limits: Messaging, enforcement and engineering not separated; pedestrian result not cyclist effect.
access: Original full government-commissioned report

authors: Richmond, S. A.; Zhang, Y. J.; Stover, A.; Howard, A.; Macarthur, C.
title: Prevention of bicycle-related injuries in children and youth: a systematic review of bicycle skills training interventions
design: Systematic review of 16 databases; included observational and experimental bicycle-skill and safety-education studies; quality assessed with Downs and Black criteria.
sample: 25 studies involving children under 19; 16 measured knowledge and 13 behavior or attitudes.
endpoint: Injury, knowledge, behavior and attitude outcomes in bicycle skills and safety-education studies.
finding: Review found no clear evidence of injury reduction. Eight of 16 studies reported knowledge gains; five of 13 reported behavior or attitude improvement. No clear relationship between study quality and those improvements.
limits: Heterogeneous interventions and designs; review reports study counts rather than a pooled injury effect. Sparse high-quality evidence; null does not prove all training is ineffective.
access: Full original journal PDF supplied by reader; abstract and Results/Discussion checked

authors: Skivington, K.; et al.
title: A new framework for developing and evaluating complex interventions: update of Medical Research Council guidance
design: Methods and guidance framework
sample: Not an effectiveness sample
endpoint: Evaluation design, context and program theory
finding: Develop and evaluate interventions iteratively in context.
limits: Guidance, not a cyclist messaging effect estimate.
access: Open full methods article

authors: Embree, T. E.; Romanow, N. T. R.; Djerboua, M. S.; Morgunov, N. J.; Bourdeaux, J. J.; Hagel, B. E.
title: Risk Factors for Bicycling Injuries in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review
design: Systematic review of comparative studies published 1990–May 2015; bicyclists younger than 20; risk of bias assessed with Newcastle-Ottawa scales.
sample: 14 articles; heterogeneous populations, exposures and injury definitions.
endpoint: Bicycle injuries and associated risk factors among children and adolescents.
finding: Lower socioeconomic status, on-road riding, riding in rural versus urban areas, and sidewalk riding were associated with bicycle injury. The review found that bicycle safety education did not protect children against future injury in the included evidence. Motor-vehicle collision injuries were more severe.
limits: Study heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis; study quality was affected by unclear group definitions and self-reported data. Observational risk associations do not establish causal effects of education.
access: Full original journal PDF supplied by reader; abstract, results and discussion checked

authors: Goddard, T.; Ralph, K.; Thigpen, C. G.; Iacobucci, E.
title: Does news coverage of traffic crashes affect perceived blame and preferred solutions? Evidence from an experiment
design: Random assignment to one of three versions of a hypothetical news article about a fatal pedestrian crash: pedestrian-focused, driver-focused, or thematic/systemic framing.
sample: 999 U.S. participants.
endpoint: Stated allocation of blame, preferred punishment, and support for road-safety solutions.
finding: Driver-focused wording shifted average blame share toward the driver (50.2% to 65.5%) and away from the pedestrian (43.1% to 30.0%) relative to pedestrian-focused wording. The thematic frame increased stated support for pedestrian infrastructure.
limits: One hypothetical pedestrian fatality and a news article, not a cyclist PSA or real crash; judgments and policy preferences were reported, not actual driving or policy behavior.
access: Open-access full paper; DOI and publisher record available.

authors: Hels, T.; Madsen, T. K. O.; Christensen, M. C.; Tallaksen, A. B.; Lahrmann, H.
title: The effect on cyclist safety of daytime running lights
design: One-year randomized controlled trial of continuous daytime-running-light use versus usual light routine, with monthly self-reported accident surveys.
sample: 5,380 volunteers randomized; 3,592 submitted at least one monthly survey; 230 accidents reported.
endpoint: Self-reported cyclist accidents per participant-month, including multi-party and personal-injury accidents.
finding: After reporting-bias correction, all multi-party accidents had IRR .70 (95% CI .39–1.28) and multi-party personal-injury accidents IRR .75 (.23–2.47), neither significant. Multi-party accidents in darkness had IRR .29 (.10–.84), a significant subgroup result.
limits: Voluntary convenience sample; incomplete monthly survey response and self-reported accidents; wide confidence intervals. The dark subgroup result may reflect better nighttime lighting in the test group. This tests equipment use, not a public message encouraging it.
access: Open full peer-reviewed article and institutional record.

authors: Keppner, V.; Krumpoch, S.; Kob, R.; Rappl, A.; Sieber, C. C.; Freiberger, E.; Siebentritt, H. M.
title: Safer cycling in older age (SiFAr): effects of a multi-component cycle training. A randomized controlled trial
design: Parallel-group randomized controlled trial of eight cycling-exercise sessions over three months versus active health-advice control; standardized practical cycling course assessed before/after and at 6–9 months.
sample: 127 adults aged 65+ randomized; 96 analyzed for primary outcome (47 intervention, 49 active control), mean age 73.4 years; participants were e-bike beginners, self-reported unsteady, or returning after a longer break.
endpoint: Errors on a standardized practical cycling course after training and at 6–9 months.
finding: Adjusted intervention effect was B=−2.51 fewer course errors after intervention (95% CI −4.05 to −0.96) and B=−3.02 at 6–9 months (−4.91 to −1.14). A separate unadjusted long-term model reported B=−3.07; do not label that as the adjusted result.
limits: Standardized course skill outcome, not road crashes or injuries; course assessor not blinded; selected older adults with self-perceived training needs; 31 randomized participants not in primary-outcome analysis.
access: Open full-text randomized trial

authors: World Health Organization
title: Road Safety Mass Media Campaigns: A Toolkit
design: Official WHO campaign-planning toolkit; publication year follows the original PDF and its suggested citation
sample: Not a cycling trial
endpoint: Campaign development and delivery
finding: Use audience research, implementation planning and evaluation.
limits: Toolkit experience spans other road-safety topics; not cyclist-specific effect.
access: Full original WHO toolkit PDF; 2016 publication, website listing dated 2019

authors: World Health Organization
title: Cyclist safety: an information resource for decision-makers and practitioners
design: Official practitioner resource
sample: Not an intervention sample
endpoint: Safe System and cyclist safety planning
finding: Combine behavioral measures with safer systems.
limits: Practice guidance; not independent evidence that a message works.
access: Full original WHO practitioner-resource PDF; 2020 edition

authors: Yadav, R.-P.; Kobayashi, M.
title: A systematic review: effectiveness of mass media campaigns for reducing alcohol-impaired driving and alcohol-related crashes
design: Systematic review with pooled injury/fatality analysis
sample: 19 studies; 7 pooled
endpoint: Alcohol-related injury/fatality crashes
limits: Indirect for cycling; heterogeneous media/enforcement packages and before-after designs.
access: Original open review and indexed abstract

authors: Delhomme, P.; et al. (eds.)
title: Manual for Designing, Implementing, and Evaluating Road Safety Communication Campaigns, Part II: Deliverable 3.2b
design: European CAST project practical campaign-planning manual; guidance synthesis, not intervention evaluation
sample: 146-page public final Part II manual
endpoint: Campaign planning, pretesting, implementation, process/outcome/economic evaluation
finding: Describes a six-step planning cycle and recommends audience research, pretesting for clarity/appropriateness/appeal, and evaluation planning before launch.
limits: Guidance is not a controlled test of any cyclist message or an estimate of injury reduction.
access: Official Vias-hosted full 146-page PDF, also supplied by reader.

authors: Dunn, N.; Greatbatch, R.; Radlbeck, J.; La Rose, C.; Bravo Bueno, J.
title: Evaluating Traffic Safety Campaigns: A Guide
design: Practice guide and evaluation framework; BTSCRP Research Report 14
sample: No intervention sample; guidance for state highway safety offices and other campaign evaluators
endpoint: Campaign awareness/reach, knowledge, attitudes, intentions, behavior, and long-term safety outcomes
finding: Sets out formative, process, outcome, and impact evaluation; recommends matching metrics and methods to campaign goals and combining surveys/media metrics with observed behavior, citation, or crash data when appropriate. Awareness and knowledge alone do not establish behavior change. (PDF pp. 12–14; report pp. 2–4)
limits: Guidance, not an effectiveness trial or cyclist-specific evidence review; US state highway safety office focus. Cost estimates are ranges and require local adaptation.
access: Official National Academies page and full report PDF; 152 pp.

authors: Dunn, N.; Greatbatch, R.; Radlbeck, J.; La Rose, C.; Bravo Bueno, J.
title: Objectives, Components, and Measures of Effective Traffic Safety Public Awareness and Education Efforts
design: Conduct-of-research report documenting a phased literature/environmental scan and toolkit development
sample: 40 sources: 21 peer-reviewed studies, 17 reports, one web page, and one book chapter; traffic safety campaigns mainly in the US
endpoint: Evaluation methods and metrics used for campaign exposure, awareness, knowledge, attitudes, intentions, behavior, and crashes
finding: Identifies measures and their limits and documents the research behind the companion guide. Search initially targeted 2013–2023 US campaigns, then broadened to 1995–2012 and health-communication campaigns when few sources were found. (PDF p. 13)
limits: Not a campaign trial or systematic effectiveness review. Search was a rapid scan (screened result batches until no new relevant sources); toolkit materials were not reviewed by intended SHSO users or subject-matter experts. (PDF pp. 13–14, 40)
access: Official National Academies page; full Web-Only Document 7 PDF, 150 pp.

authors: Phillips, D.; Mohammed, S.; Rantanen, K.; Bury, J.; Sayers, E.; Forsyth, E.; Bertasevicius, V.; Eyers, J.
title: Cycling and Walking Safety: A rapid evidence assessment for the Department for Transport
design: Rapid evidence assessment; narrative synthesis
sample: 114 eligible documents; 51 prioritized for synthesis (24 evidence reviews and 27 quantitative primary studies); 4 synthesized studies addressed road-user education
endpoint: Risk/perceived risk and participation for cycling and walking interventions
finding: Synthesis found only a small, mixed education-campaign evidence base: the randomized Gamble leaflet study changed neither perceived risk nor cycling intention; a THINK! poster pre/post study reported some increased claimed cyclist-safe behaviors; the report concludes evidence is insufficient for firm education-effect conclusions. (PDF pp. 17–18, 36–37; report pp. 14–15, 34–35)
limits: Report cover is dated 17 Sep 2018; GOV.UK publication date is 7 Feb 2020. Single-reviewer screening/data extraction, machine-learning prioritization and synthesis of only 51/114 eligible items limit completeness; only five studies measured both risk and participation. Not a campaign meta-analysis. (PDF pp. 5–7, 12–18; report pp. 3–5, 10–15)
access: Official GOV.UK record and full NatCen report PDF; 80 pp.

authors: Faus, M.; Alonso, F.; Fernández, C.; Useche, S. A.
title: Are Traffic Announcements Really Effective? A Systematic Review of Evaluations of Crash-Prevention Communication Campaigns
design: PRISMA-described systematic mapping/narrative review; no meta-analysis
sample: 27 campaign evaluations selected from 613 records; 24 observational/nonexperimental, 2 experimental, and 1 mixed-method study
endpoint: Attitudes, knowledge, self-reported road-user behavior, and crash outcomes across heterogeneous road-safety campaigns
finding: Reports mixed results: some campaign effects, often temporary; communication tended to perform better alongside legislation or road-safety education. Ten campaigns targeted drink-driving; the review does not establish a cyclist-specific message effect. (PDF pp. 11–14)
limits: Selection involved removing duplicates and inaccessible papers plus manual fit decisions; no reproducible risk-of-bias tool or study-quality ratings are reported in the article. Outcomes and campaigns are highly heterogeneous; co-interventions limit attribution. Do not describe the review as having a formal quality appraisal.
access: Open publisher full text and local candidate PDF; Safety 7(4):66.

authors: Fisa, R.; Musukuma, M.; Sampa, M.; Musonda, P.; Young, T.
title: Effects of interventions for preventing road traffic crashes: an overview of systematic reviews
design: Overview of systematic reviews; descriptive synthesis; AMSTAR 2 appraisal
sample: 35 reviews; five evaluated public-awareness campaigns; 33/35 reviews included studies only from high-income countries
endpoint: Road traffic crashes involving a moving vehicle; awareness campaign findings are not cyclist-specific
finding: The five awareness reviews included three rated critically low quality and two moderate quality. The reported 9% campaign crash reduction is inherited from Phillips et al. (2011), not a new pooled estimate by Fisa et al. (PDF pp. 6, 11, 16)
limits: Excludes crashes without a motor vehicle; evidence is dominated by high-income settings and review quality is generally weak. Fisa’s abstract gives the Phillips campaign interval as −11% to −8%, whereas Phillips et al. report −12% to −6%; use the original Phillips estimate if cited. (PDF pp. 1, 11, 16)
access: Open BMC full text and local candidate PDF; 18 pp.

authors: Stefanidis, K. B.; Davey, B.; Truelove, V.; Schiemer, C.; Freeman, J.
title: Does exposure to social media content influence attitudes towards, and engagement in, road rule violations? A systematic review
design: PRISMA systematic review; qualitative synthesis
sample: 8 English-language peer-reviewed studies; seven content analyses and one focus-group study; searches in four databases to June 2021
endpoint: Social-media road-rule content and its potential relationship to attitudes/behavior; predominantly motor-vehicle driving, not cycling
finding: Review finds risky-driving content online but the evidence cannot establish its effects: the sole exposure/behavior study used focus groups with young men and did not directly measure exposure-related behavior change. (PDF pp. 1, 3, 10–11)
limits: No meta-analysis or risk-of-bias appraisal; excludes grey literature, and the included studies focus on few platforms/topics. Not evidence that cyclist-safety messaging on social media changes behavior. (PDF pp. 2–3, 11)
access: Open PLOS full text and local candidate PDF; 13 pp.

authors: Winters, M.; Weddell, A.; Teschke, K.
title: Is Evidence in Practice? Review of Driver and Cyclist Education Materials with Respect to Cycling Safety Evidence
design: Cycling-safety evidence review paired with a content audit; no intervention evaluation
sample: 56 safety studies and 48 education materials from Canadian driver-licensing jurisdictions, municipalities, and advocacy groups
endpoint: Alignment of cyclist/driver education content with cycling-safety evidence on operations, visibility, road characteristics, routes, and interactions with motor vehicles
finding: Most material topics aligned with the evidence; the authors flagged conflicting guidance about motor-vehicle passing distance/where to ride and a gap in guidance on relative safety of route infrastructure. Useful as a copy-accuracy check, not proof that education changes outcomes. (PDF pp. 1–3; journal pp. 35–38)
limits: Canadian material inventory; one author categorized materials and a subset was checked by another. Safety evidence search used one primary screener, excluded helmet-only studies and subjective safety perceptions, and did not formally critique study methods. (PDF pp. 2–3; journal pp. 36–37)
access: TRB article full text hosted by UBC; TRR 2387, pp. 35–45.

authors: Nachman, E. R.; Rodriguez, D. A.
title: Evaluating the effects of a classroom-based bicycle education intervention on bicycle activity, self-efficacy, personal safety, knowledge, and mode choice
design: Staggered within-person pre/post (case-crossover) panel evaluation of a 2-hour classroom course; not-yet-trained participants supplied same-period comparisons; no random assignment or never-trained control.
sample: 31 classes in nine San Francisco Bay Area cities; current-study survey: 182 baseline, 113 paired; supplemental prior survey: 201 baseline, 45 paired; total 158 paired participants
endpoint: Self-reported bicycling activity, confidence, perceived safety, rules knowledge, and travel mode; Ride Report app used for a small validation subsample
finding: Course participation was associated with higher confidence, car-free-area safety, and rules knowledge; no significant overall change in bicycle trip count. Ride Report agreement check was small (n=12 before; n=11 after removing an outlier), not an objective primary outcome. (PDF pp. 5–8)
limits: Self-selected Bay Area course attendees, substantial follow-up attrition (current sample 40%; supplemental 78%), underpowered relative to target, no control group or crash outcomes; subgroup results exploratory. Training evidence, not a campaign-copy test. (PDF pp. 5, 13–14)
access: Open Frontiers full text and local candidate PDF; 16 pp.

authors: Schönbach, D. M. I.; Altenburg, T. M.; Marques, A.; Chinapaw, M. J. M.; Demetriou, Y.
title: Strategies and effects of school-based interventions to promote active school transportation by bicycle among children and adolescents: a systematic review
design: PRISMA systematic review of controlled trials; narrative synthesis
sample: 9 studies evaluating 7 interventions (2012–2018); ages up to 17; search across 8 databases
endpoint: Active school travel, psychosocial/physical-activity outcomes, and cycling skills; not injury or crash prevention
finding: All nine studies were rated weak quality. Seven favorable outcomes across two studies came from the same adult-guided bicycle-train intervention; overall evidence was judged insufficient, with that program only a promising strategy. (PDF pp. 1–2, 6–9, 14–15)
limits: Highly heterogeneous outcomes precluded meta-analysis; selection bias, blinding, and intervention integrity were weak, contamination common, and adolescent/secondary-school evidence sparse. Not campaign evidence. (PDF pp. 5–6, 14–15)
access: Open BMC full text and local candidate PDF; 17 pp.

authors: Gamble, T.; Walker, I.; Laketa, A.
title: Bicycling campaigns promoting health versus campaigns promoting safety: A randomized controlled online study of ‘dangerization’
design: Randomized online pre/post experiment: safety leaflet, health leaflet, or neutral control
sample: 228 adults recruited opportunistically online; 159 had cycled in prior two weeks and 69 had not
endpoint: Immediate perceived cycling risk, health benefits, enjoyment, and stated intention to cycle
finding: Health leaflet increased non-cyclists’ perceived health benefits; safety leaflet changed neither perceived risk nor health benefits. Neither leaflet changed stated cycling intention or enjoyment. (PDF pp. 3, 10–13)
limits: Immediate post-exposure outcomes measured minutes after one online leaflet; no behavior, participation, or crash endpoint and no check that participants read/understood the leaflet. Convenience sample, self-reports, and a broad cyclist definition limit generalization. Authors’ enjoyment-message suggestion was not tested. (PDF pp. 3, 16–17)
access: Peer-reviewed manuscript full text from University of Bath; published in Journal of Transport & Health 2(3), 369–378.

authors: Sundfør, H. B.; Phillips, R. O.; Aasvik, O.
title: Evaluation of the Norwegian Public Roads Administration’s campaign ‘Most people follow the speed limit’: A norm-based approach to increasing speed compliance
design: Nonrandomized campaign evaluation using repeated nationally representative surveys and objective speed observations
sample: National survey waves and observed speeds across 2019–2025; sample sizes not stated in the one-page English summary; full report is 103 pp in Norwegian
endpoint: Norm perceptions, attitudes, intentions/self-reported speeding, and observed speed-limit compliance
finding: Exposure was most clearly associated with perceived social norms; attitudes improved without a consistent exposure association, and speed observations indicated increased compliance. No control group means effects cannot be causally attributed to the campaign. (English summary, p. 1)
limits: Not cycling-specific; local English full text is only a one-page summary, so samples, analyses, and estimates could not be independently checked here. Official TØI page links the full Norwegian report.
access: Official TØI publication page, English summary PDF, and linked Norwegian report.

authors: Tyagi, S.; Wragg, N.; Suhendra, F.
title: That resonated with me: A user-centred approach to understanding young adult vulnerable road users’ road safety campaigns messaging needs—Case study
design: Qualitative user-centered case study using workshops
sample: 30 young adult vulnerable road users in Australia; workshop participants
endpoint: Audience interpretation and preferences for campaign messages
finding: Participants described value in specific, purposeful, actionable instructions and highlighted multiple road-user roles and intersectional identities.
limits: Qualitative formative findings are not a test of message effects on driving, riding, crashes, or injuries. Transfer to other age groups or settings needs testing.
access: Open publisher article page and indexed abstract; no local full-text PDF obtained.

authors: Limb, M.; Collyer, S.
title: The effect of safety attire on perceptions of cyclist dehumanisation
design: Self-selected online image-perception experiment with paired forced-choice photographs
sample: 563 survey respondents in Australia; nonrepresentative convenience sample
endpoint: Ratings or choices of perceived cyclist humanity in photographs
finding: Photographs of cyclists in helmets or safety vests were more likely to be selected as less human than photographs without safety attire.
limits: Perception ratings are not observed driver behavior or injury; self-selected sample limits generalization. Do not infer that riders should avoid protective equipment.
access: Full article PDF in research collection; indexed journal record.

authors: Torres-Barragán, C. A.; Cottrill, C. D.; Beecroft, M.
title: Spatial inequalities and media representation of cycling safety in Bogotá, Colombia
design: Spatial and archival case study of local crash reporting, infrastructure, and socioeconomic patterns
sample: Bogotá newspaper accounts of cyclist deaths/injuries, 2002–2017
endpoint: Place and media representation of cyclist harm
finding: Reports and safety conditions were uneven across places and social groups, motivating attention to whose risks and experiences a campaign represents.
limits: Single-city observational case study; newspaper coverage is an incomplete crash source and no message intervention was tested.
access: Open publisher full article page and indexed TRID record.

authors: Ferenchak, N. N.; Sanchez Rodriguez, O.; Losada-Rojas, L. L.; Schneider, R.; Gu, X.
title: Longitudinal socioeconomic and built environment shifts in US bicyclist fatality locations 2001–2020
design: Longitudinal census-tract analysis of U.S. bicyclist fatalities and neighborhood context
sample: FARS fatality locations, 2001–2020; census and EPA spatial variables
endpoint: Area-level fatality locations and correlates
finding: Fatality locations shifted toward lower-density areas; tracts with fatalities had distinct socioeconomic characteristics relative to national averages.
limits: Area-level associations are not individual risk estimates or message effects; commute data imperfectly measures bicycling exposure and road speed/volume were unavailable nationally.
access: Open publisher full article under Creative Commons license.

authors: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
title: Communicating Safe Behavior Practices to Vulnerable Road Users
design: BTSCRP Web-Only Document 6; practitioner toolkit and planning guidance
sample: 192-page report; not an intervention sample
endpoint: Audience, channel, and campaign design methods for vulnerable road users
finding: Provides tools for identifying safety problems, audience needs, feasible behavioral targets, and communication channels.
limits: Guidance and component examples do not establish that any particular print message reduces cyclist crashes or injuries.
access: Official National Academies online full text; PDF download requires guest or account access.

authors: Høye, A.; Fyhri, A.; Bjørnskau, T.
title: Shared road is double happiness: Evaluation of a Share the Road sign
design: Before/after roadside surveys on a test road and a comparison road near Oslo
sample: Cyclists and car drivers recruited on two roads
endpoint: Self-reported and perceived behaviors; sign awareness
finding: Reported passing behavior improved on the test road relative to comparison road
limits: Season and respondent composition varied; primarily recreational traffic; outcomes were reported behavior, not measured passing distance
access: Full author manuscript in local research collection

authors: Dalton, A.; Sumner, F.; Jones, A.
title: Digital screen use for a road safety campaign message was not associated with attitudes or knowledge of passers-by: an experimental study
design: Quasi-experiment comparing control and screen-exposure days
sample: 364 public interview respondents over five days
endpoint: Reported message awareness, recall and attitudes
finding: 364 interviews over five days; image displayed on two intervention days. No significant intervention-day difference in priority ranking or recall of the numeric claim. Survey outcomes after brief exposure, not driving or injuries.
limits: Short exposure and survey responses; no direct observation of driving behavior
access: University repository abstract and author accepted manuscript

authors: Bacchieri, G.; Barros, A. J. D.; dos Santos, J. V.; Gonçalves, H.; Gigante, D. P.
title: A community intervention to prevent traffic accidents among bicycle commuters
design: Stepped-wedge community intervention with monthly telephone follow-up
sample: 1133 adult male bicycle commuters in Pelotas, Brazil
endpoint: Self-reported traffic crashes and near-crashes per cyclist-month
finding: After adjusting for time the study found no statistically significant protective effect on crashes or near-crashes
limits: Approximately 45% did not attend; self-report; combined educational, equipment and brake-check package; context and secular trends affect interpretation
access: Full original journal article PDF

authors: Houts, P. S.; Doak, C. C.; Doak, L. G.; Loscalzo, M. J.
title: The role of pictures in improving health communication: A review of research on attention, comprehension, recall, and adherence
design: Narrative review of health-communication, psychology, education and marketing research
sample: Varied populations and interventions
endpoint: Attention, comprehension, recall and adherence
finding: Pictures closely paired with text can support attention, recall and comprehension; spatial and relational diagrams can help understanding
limits: Indirect for cycling; heterogeneous interventions and outcomes; narrative review, not a cycling-campaign effect estimate
access: Full published article PDF from University of Trieste repository; sections 4 and 8 checked

authors: Calderón, R.; Sheveland, A.; Outman, M.; Sharma, A.
title: A Nationwide Review of Pedestrian and Bicyclist Safety Education in Driver Education
design: Structured content audit of driver-education resources
sample: Methods pp. 3-4: 31 curriculum guides across 30 states; 50 manuals (49 states and DC); 11 training resources. Discussion p. 27 instead gives 49 manuals and 13 trainings.
endpoint: Coverage of pedestrian and bicyclist safety topics in education materials
finding: Coverage varied. Manuals emphasized rules over safe-driving practices; many training resources omitted newer facilities such as bike boxes. Use to identify local teaching gaps.
limits: Content audit, not an intervention trial. Methods and discussion disagree on manual/training counts; narrative report omits totals. No estimate of changes in driving or injuries.
access: Full original NHTSA report DOT HS 813 655; local copy from Pedestrian and Bicycle Information Center; methods pp. 3-4 and discussion pp. 27-28 checked
